apply.sh + apply.ps1 both add a post-copy stamp/strip step gated on agents.claude=true, looping over exactly the 5 named files (docs-sync, test-gap-advisor, dependency-auditor, performance-advisor, onboarder) - every other subagent .md is never referenced by the loop so it's structurally impossible to touch them. Algorithm (shared design, ported line-for-line to awk in .sh and to a PowerShell function in .ps1): locate frontmatter between the first two '---' lines, insert/replace/remove a single 'model: haiku' line, preserving each file's own EOL style. Verified: this sandbox denies bash -n/pwsh execution outright (confirmed via direct Bash, PowerShell, and a delegated subagent - filed aiflow-hj6), so I ported the exact algorithm to a throwaway Node.js script (Node is wildcard-allowed here) and ran it against the 5 REAL template files unmodified on disk (read-only): confirmed add inserts the line before the closing --- with the file's real EOL (discovered mid-verification that dependency-auditor.md/performance-advisor.md are actually plain-LF while docs-sync/test-gap-advisor/onboarder are CRLF - good thing the algorithm detects per-file rather than assuming one style repo-wide), add-twice is idempotent, strip removes it, strip-twice is idempotent, and add-then-strip round-trips to byte-identical original. Also confirmed all 10 other agent files exist and are never passed to the stamp function. Both .sh/.ps1 implementations were then manually cross-checked line-by-line against this verified algorithm for behavioral parity. Live bash/pwsh execution of apply.sh/apply.ps1 themselves deferred to a human/interactive session.
